text: One direct flight of 4 to 6 hours from India and you're cruising past around 1600 limestone islands rising out of an emerald sea. That's Halong Bay and it's just one corner of Vietnam. Lantern-lit old towns, rice terraces carved into mountains, beaches straight out of a screensaver, and food that will spoil every other noodle soup for you. Namaste and welcome to Trust and Trip. In the next 10 minutes, you'll know exactly when to go, where to go, where to stay, what to eat, and how to get around. And stay till the end because I'll share the three mistakes that ruin most first trips to Vietnam. First, the basics. Vietnam is long and thin, stretching about 1650 km from north to south, shaped like the letter S. That's why Hanoi and Ho Chi Minh City can have completely different weather on the very same day. So, here's the simple rule. The north, Hanoi, Halong, and Sapa is best from October to April, but pack a jacket because December and January get properly chilly. The center, Hoi An and Da Nang, is best from February to August. Avoid October to December there. That's the heavy rain season. And the south, Saigon and Phu Quoc, is sunniest from December to April. Want one sweet spot for the whole country? Go in March or April. Now, getting there. There are direct flights from Indian cities like Delhi, Mumbai, and Kolkata to Hanoi and Ho Chi Minh City, usually 4 to 6 hours in the air. Fly into one city and out of the other so you never waste a day backtracking. For the visa, Indians can apply online for a Vietnam e-visa. The official government fee is $25 US dollars for single entry and $50 for multiple entry valid for up to 90 days. It usually takes a few working days, so apply at least 2 weeks before you fly and only on the official government portal. More on that in the mistakes section. Let's travel north to south. Start in Hanoi, the 1,000-year-old capital. Base yourself in the Old Quarter, walk around Hoan Kiem Lake in the morning, and sit on a tiny plastic stool with a glass of iced tea. It's a Hanoi ritual. Don't miss the Temple of Literature, founded in 1070 and home to Vietnam's first university. Then, about 3 hours by road takes you to Ha Long Bay. Here's my tip. Skip the rushed day trip and book an overnight cruise. You'll kayak into hidden lagoons, explore the caves, and wake up to sunrise over the islands after the day trippers have gone. For quieter waters, ask for a route through Lan Ha Bay. From Hanoi, take a day trip to Ninh Binh, often called Ha Long Bay on land. In Trang An, a local rower takes you by boat through limestone caves and rice fields. And if you climb the 500 steps up Mua Cave, you get one of the best views in Vietnam. Love mountains? Head to Sapa in the far north. Trek through rice terraces with local guides and take the cable car up Fansipan. At 3,143 m, it's the highest peak in all of Indochina. Sapa's terraces are greenest from June to August and turn golden September just before the harvest. Now, fly about an hour and a quarter south to Da Nang, the gateway to central Vietnam. Up in the Ba Na Hills is the Golden Bridge held up by two giant hands. And on weekend nights, Da Nang's Dragon Bridge actually breathes fire and water. Just 45 minutes away is Hoi An, a UNESCO World Heritage Old Town. By day, get clothes stitched by local tailor, often within a day or two. By night, the whole town glows with silk lanterns, and you can float a paper lantern on the river. Got an extra day? Hue, the old royal capital with its Imperial Citadel, is a few hours north. Here's something most people skip. Between Hue and Hanoi lies Phong Nha Ke Bang National Park, home to some of the most spectacular caves on Earth. Paradise Cave runs for about 31 km, and a wooden walkway takes you deep inside. This is also where you'll find Son Doong, the largest cave in the world, so big it has its own jungle, and even its own clouds inside. Only a small number of permitted expeditions enter Son Doong each year, but the nearby caves are open to everyone, and you can even zipline straight into the Dark Cave for a swim in the mud. Finally, the South. Ho Chi Minh City, still called Saigon by most locals, runs on motorbikes and coffee. See the Old Central Post Office, the War Remnants Museum, and crawl through the Cu Chi tunnels, a network of around 250 km dug by hand during the war. Take a day trip into the Mekong Delta for floating markets, coconut candy workshops, and life on the river. And end your trip on Phu Quoc Island with white sand beaches, golden sunsets, and one of the world's longest sea crossing cable cars, gliding almost 8 km over the water to Hon Thom Island. So, where should you stay? Think area first, hotel second. In Hanoi, stay in the Old Quarter or near Hoan Kiem Lake, so everything is walkable. In Ha Long, your cruise is your hotel. In Hoi An, stay at the edge of the old town for the lanterns or at An Bang Beach for peace and quiet. In Da Nang, pick a sea view hotel along My Khe Beach. In Saigon, stay in District 1 and in Phu Quoc, choose the west coast for the sunsets. Every area has three levels: friendly family-run homestays, stylish boutique hotels, and full-on luxury resorts. Tell us your budget and we'll match the right one. Now, the best part, the food. Start with pho, the famous noodle soup at breakfast, just like the locals do. In Hanoi, try bun cha, grilled pork with noodles, the dish Barack Obama and Anthony Bourdain shared on plastic stools. In Hoi An, eat a banh mi, the crispy Vietnamese baguette, and the town's own noodle dish, cao lau. Don't leave without an egg coffee, invented in Hanoi in the 1940s, and creamy like a dessert. Vegetarian? Look for the word chay. It means vegetarian and chay restaurants are easy to find. And yes, the big cities have Indian restaurants, too, for when you miss your dal. Getting around is easier than you think. Download the Grab app before you land. It works like Uber for cars, motorbike taxis, and even food with the price shown up front, so no haggling. For long distances, take domestic flights. They're quick and frequent between Hanoi, Da Nang, and Saigon. Have more time? The overnight sleeper train along the coast is an experience in itself. Sleeper buses are the cheapest option, and in Hoi An, just rent a bicycle. One golden rule for crossing the road, walk slowly and steadily. Don't run and don't stop. The motorbikes will flow around you, act them like water. A few quick money and phone tips. The currency is the Vietnamese dong and the notes have a lot of zeros. The 20,000 and the 500,000 notes are both blue, so check twice before you pay. Exchange money at a bank or an authorized counter in the city where rates are usually better than at the airport and cards work in most hotels and malls. Pick up a local SIM or an e-SIM when you land. It's cheap and gives you data for Grab and maps everywhere. Tipping isn't compulsory, but a small tip for a great guide or driver is always appreciated. Here's a simple 9-day plan. Three nights in Hanoi with a day trip to Ninh Binh, one night on a Ha Long Bay cruise, two nights in Hoi An with a day in Da Nang, and two nights in Saigon with a Mekong Delta day trip. Add Phu Quoc if you have three more days. Now, the three mistakes. One, fake visa websites. Many look official and charge extra, so use only the government portal. Two, trying to see everything in one week. Pick two regions or fly between them. Three, ignoring the weather. Central Vietnam's rains from October to December can wash out your beach days, so plan by region. And if you'd rather not plan all of this yourself, that's exactly what we do.
